1.pericope_label: My soul is weary of my life: I will say unto God, do not condemn me; show me wherefore thou contendest with me

schools.summary: Gill measures how strange the weariness is, since no temporal blessing is more desirable than life, and rules out the usual causes of it; on the petition he denies that eternal condemnation was ever the fear, since there is none for those in Christ, and would render the words do not account me wicked, that is, do not treat me so by keeping the afflicting hand upon me.

Henry traces the speech to a man daunted by God’s majesty who cannot plead his cause and so eases himself by venting resentment, draws the line between violent hands and violent words, hears grace put in a word when the complaint is left upon the complainer, and reads the prayer as asking to lie under the cross and not the curse, adding the rule that when God afflicts he contends and when he contends there is always a cause.

Clarke draws from the word for soul a proof that Job was no materialist but credited the immortality of the soul, and supplies the alternatives Job does not consider, that God afflicts only for past sin, or to try his followers, or to show his grace in delivering them; Wesley reduces the opening to a question put to himself, concedes that God might deal so in rigorous justice, and asks that integrity be shown by removing the stroke.

Ellicott reports a reading that gives free vent to the complaint and calls the petition a model of prayer joining the publican’s plea to a plea for light; Delitzsch finds the motive in self-consciousness, a man who has renounced all claim on a life he is weary of and will at least let his complaints run their course, praying that the Author of his sufferings not let him die the death of the wicked.

debates.question: Why was he weary of his life?

sides.position: not from guilt pressing him as with Cain and Judas, nor from indwelling sin, nor from grief at the sins of others, but from the state of the body itself
because, daunted by God’s majesty, he could not plead his cause, and so went against the dictates of nature through weakness of grace
the question is what the word for soul proves, namely that he meant the immortal mind and not animal life

debates.question: What does do not condemn me ask for?

sides.position: not escape from eternal condemnation, impossible for those in Christ, but that God not account him wicked by keeping the afflicting hand upon him
that he be spared the sting of the affliction, lying under the cross and not the curse
that he not be made to die the death of the wicked against the testimony of his own conscience
it is a model of prayer for everyone, joining the publican’s plea to the plea for light

outliers: Gill alone refuses to read the hands and the pronouns of this passage as the Son and the Spirit, calling it too great a strain on the words.
Henry alone presses the duty of self-restraint in complaint, that wisdom and grace are given us to keep the mouth as with a bridle.
themes: a life its owner has fallen out with
complaint kept short of accusation
the curse feared more than the cross
a reason asked for, not a reprieve

3.pericope_label: Is it good unto thee that thou shouldest oppress? Hast thou eyes of flesh, that thou enquirest after mine iniquity?

schools.summary: Gill answers the first question from God’s own conduct, since he disapproves oppression in others and promises to help the oppressed and so will never practise it, grants that the hand presses hard without injustice, says plainly that these verses take too much freedom with the Almighty, catalogues what fleshly eyes cannot do against what God’s eyes reach, and limits the final protest to a denial of hypocrisy rather than of sin.

Clarke turns the first question outward, since distressing the children of men can gratify nobody and seems to confirm the verdict of the wicked that religion brings no benefit, finds the argument about days in the Hebrew’s two different words for man, and asks whether it befits infinite dignity to concern itself with a despicable mortal’s transgressions; Wesley keeps both sides, far from thinking God wronged him yet unable to reconcile the providences with the justice, and explains why eternity needs no scrutiny where a short life must hurry its inquiries.
Ellicott sharpens the last claim from a character to a verdict, that he shall not be found guilty, and distinguishes it from the appeal of Peter.

debates.question: Do the questions about eyes and days deny the likeness or only distinguish it?

sides.position: they distinguish: fleshly eyes are bounded by distance, place, darkness and surface, while God’s reach everywhere and into the heart
the Hebrew uses one word for wretched mortal man and another for the strong man, so neither man at his lowest nor at his best can be set beside God

debates.question: What does thou knowest that I am not wicked claim?

sides.position: not sinlessness, already confessed, but that he is not the hypocrite his friends suppose, one over whom sin has dominion
not a character but a verdict, that he shall not be found guilty
that God is sifting him as though to find sin, and treating him as a transgressor when none can be found

outliers: Gill alone rebukes the speaker he is expounding, saying the expostulations of these verses take too much freedom with the Almighty.
Clarke alone observes that the complaint about God troubling himself with a despicable mortal is a word spoken in the heart of most sinners.
themes: oppression weighed against God’s own law
eyes that cannot be deceived
a trial prolonged by one who needs no evidence
innocence claimed only of hypocrisy

8.pericope_label: Thine hands have made me and fashioned me: thou hast granted me life and favour, and these things hast thou hid in thine heart

schools.summary: Gill says the passage exists to move compassion, since not the man nor his parents but God only made him, so that the hands which formed him are the hands none can deliver out of; he declines to read those hands of the Son and the Spirit, as some do, calling it too great a strain on the words.

Henry follows the formation step by step, the body cast as a potter casts clay so that we are earthen vessels neither to be proud of nor to be dishonoured, skin and flesh for clothing and bones and sinews for defensive armour, then counts life and favour as two gifts and has God keep the lamp supplied with fresh oil, and turns the remembering into an argument usable both as an inducement to duty and as a plea for mercy.

Clarke insists against learned men who confine the image to nutrition that generation is the true notion, leaving his Latin authorities untranslated, and makes continued visitation the reason any man’s life is preserved; Wesley calls the description modest and accurate, man congealed by degrees from a liquid and as it were milky substance, itemises what came with the life, and puts the question the passage builds towards, whether one who has been a monument of mercy is to be made a spectacle of vengeance.
Ellicott needs four words for the embryo and one sentence for the last verse, where he hears the sense of goodness embittered because God had these trials in reserve while he was showering good.

debates.question: What is poured me out as milk?

sides.position: generation, not nutrition: the chyle reading fails because that process properly begins only after birth
an allusion to the embryo
man made from a small liquid and as it were milky substance, congealed by degrees into the frame of the body

debates.question: What was hidden in God’s heart?

sides.position: the trials held in reserve while the kindness was being shown, which embitters the sense of the goodness
gracious purposes not yet made known, the visitations and mercy being proof enough of kindness
both the former favours and the present frowns, which are of one will and therefore consistent however they seem

outliers: Clarke alone presses the Hebrew of the next clause, which says not destroy but swallow up, and observes that men ordinarily prize the works they have spent most pains on.
Henry alone turns the plea into a double use, the same fact serving as an inducement to duty when pressed on ourselves and as an argument for mercy when pressed on God.
themes: a maker argued with from his own workmanship
the embryo as evidence
life counted a favour before its comforts
a purpose kept hidden on purpose

14.pericope_label: If I sin, then thou markest me: thou huntest me as a fierce lion and renewest thy witnesses against me

schools.summary: Henry is willing to call this justice bordering on severity, with conscience as God’s deputy charging each twitch of pain to a particular fault, yet insists we must acknowledge the contrary, that God does not deal with us in extremity; he takes the woe of the wicked as a warning with double force for those long under the means of grace, and finds the bitterness of the hunt in the indignation felt inside the affliction, which turns the sores of the body into wounds in the spirit.

Gill reads the marking as surveillance, every sin inquired into and laid up for another day, reports a rendering by Gussetius that turns the clause into a sacrifice offered for sin and still unregarded, puts the woe of the wicked in both worlds, and hears the affliction lifting itself in waves, noting a reading that makes the clause a wish for it to reach its height at once.

Clarke answers the second branch doctrinally, since a righteous man is only in the state his duty requires and can claim nothing from his Maker’s justice as favour, turns the lion round so that the friends are the hunters, and agrees that the whole speech is forensic; Wesley flattens the distinction as the verse does, wicked meaning the hypocrite his friends take him for and righteous an upright man, and identifies the witnesses as the judgments themselves.

Ellicott recasts the passage as a conditional in which neither guilt nor righteousness would let him lift up his head, calls the verse about increase very obscure and offers three possible subjects for it, and takes the renewed witnesses as forensic rather than physical, relays of accusers coming host after host.

debates.question: What are the witnesses renewed against him?

sides.position: relays of accusers, host after host, the ministers of a divine anger: the figure is forensic, not physical
the sores on his person, which his friends regarded as proofs of guilt
the judgments themselves, evidence at once of his sins and of God’s wrath
fresh witnesses brought in continual succession, the terms of the speech being forensic throughout

debates.question: Who is the lion, and who is hunted?

sides.position: God hunts the man, as a fierce lion runs down its prey, and shows himself marvellous upon him
the friends attack him as hunters attack the king of beasts in the forest

debates.question: What is the subject of for it increaseth?

sides.position: the affliction, which lifts itself up in waves that threaten to overwhelm, though some read the clause as a wish that it would reach its height at once
the verse is very obscure: the subject may be the affliction, or the head of the previous verse, or a question whether it is glorious to hunt a man and then hide the motive

outliers: Clarke alone reports a rendering in which God springs on the sufferer like a rousing beast of prey.
Gill alone passes on Gussetius’s rendering, by which the clause becomes a sacrifice offered for sin that was still not regarded.
themes: a fault charged to every twitch of pain
both verdicts losing
relays of witnesses
affliction that rises when the tide should ebb

18.pericope_label: Wherefore then hast thou brought me forth out of the womb? A land of darkness, as darkness itself

schools.summary: Gill ascribes the bringing forth to God as David does, notes that this is the complaint the friends had blamed and that their arguments carried no force, distinguishes what an untimely birth would and would not have been, and is at pains to deny that the going whence there is no return denies the resurrection, since the man understood that doctrine and asserts it elsewhere.

Clarke asks why being was given to one foreseen to suffer so, reads the crowd of dislocated terms as admirably expressive of a subject nobody can describe, glosses the shadow of death as a place where death rules and casts his shade and the absence of order as the levelling of rich and poor and king and beggar, gathers Sophocles and the Latin version and Coverdale for light that is as darkness, and breaks into an apostrophe on eternity; Wesley presses the shortness of the life as the plea for ease.

Ellicott marks the return to the strain of the original curse, notes a third-person reading of the request to be let alone, and judges the whole reply to move on the very verge of blasphemy, redeemed only by a pervading reverence and a deep undertone of faith.

debates.question: Does I shall not return deny the resurrection?

sides.position: no: only return to this world is denied, to a house, a family, a set of friends; the doctrine is understood and asserted elsewhere
he shall not return from the dust to have a dwelling among men again

debates.question: What is the land of darkness?

sides.position: a land of obscurity like darkness, where death rules and casts his shade and there are no distinctions of inhabitants, measured by no attribute of time
darkness itself and not merely like it, thick as the darkness of Egypt that could be felt

outliers: Ellicott alone passes a verdict on the speech as a whole, that it moves on the verge of blasphemy and is saved from it by reverence, the man wrestling like Jacob in the dark without giving up his faith.
Clarke alone leaves the commentary altogether for an apostrophe on eternity, which has no bounds, no substance and no past or present or future, and which he says he cannot know until he dies.
themes: a wish repeated after being rebuked
a hand’s breadth of days
a country with no arrangements
light that is as darkness
